author: TGEU
title: Joint LGBTI+ NGO letter to the Turkish Embassy in Berlin, Germany
content:
On 25 November, TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia, 

OII Europe

 and 

OII Germany

 have sent a joint letter to the German foreign ministries to express serious concerns about the situation in Türkiye and the recent targeting of the LGBTI+ organisations and human rights defenders.




Since 12 September, several police raids have been conducted in Türkiye, targeting LGBTI+ human rights defenders and organisations, as part of the so-called “My Family is Safe” operations. During these raids, police seized digital equipment of the activists and organisations. Websites and social media accounts of LGBTI+ activists and organisations were blocked. 78 people have been in detention for 2 months. On 23 October, in a new wave of arrests, 45 people across 7 provinces were taken into custody and more than 20 of them, including 10 trans women, were imprisoned. Again, on 3 November, 22 people were detained and questioned, several of whom are trans women, in relation to “forming an organisation for the purpose of committing a crime”. Relying on obscenity clauses and provisions on prostitution, Turkish authorities have targeted trans people and sex workers in all waves of the arrests. 




Already, in January 2026, Ankara Public Prosecutor’s Office filed a lawsuit against head of the 

17 Mayıs Association

 Defne Güzel with alleged charges of violating public morality by publishing the Turkish translation of 

OII Europe’s publication #MyIntersexStory

, a collection of testimonies of intersex people, and an exhibition catalogue. The lawsuit followed an expert report from 2025 which concluded that the activities of the 17 Mayıs Association are entirely consistent with the objectives set out in its statutes and that there are no irregularities whatsoever. Güzel was later acquitted of all charges in the first hearing in May.  




Human rights at stake




These operations mark a significant escalation in the criminalisation of LGBTI+ human rights activism in Türkiye, and a direct attack on freedom of expression, association, and the defence of human rights. The October operations criminalise non-normative identities and bodies, including trans and intersex people and organisations, based only on social media posts declared by the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office as “contrary to public morality, targeting families, children and young people, detrimental to their development, encouraging gender neutrality and disruptive to public order”.




LGBTI+ organisations in Türkiye are targeted for their legitimate activities. The domestic and international funding they receive is lawful, and they operate as registered associations under Turkish law. With these actions, the Turkish government continues to undermine the right of legally registered organisations to participate in democratic processes.




The ongoing imprisonment of 78 individuals since September, the inhumane prison conditions and the torture perpetrated against them breach international human rights law, as well as the Constitution of Türkiye and the Turkish Penal Code. The European Court of Human Rights and the UN Human Rights Committee have made clear that public morality cannot justify infringing fundamental rights. These operations also institutionalise discrimination and arbitrary detention, fuel a climate of hatred, threaten the right to life of LGBTI+ people, and increase state-sanctioned hate speech.




Germany’s role




It is clear that the rights of LGBTI+ people in Türkiye and civic freedoms enjoyed by all Turkish citizens are at stake. As a longstanding strategic partner of Türkiye and a vocal critic of Türkiye’s backsliding on rule of law, it is imperative that Germany speaks up and reminds Türkiye of its obligations as a member of the Council of Europe and a candidate country of the EU, to respect fundamental human rights standards that apply to all, no matter a person’s sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. 




As the home to the largest Turkish diaspora, Germany hosts several LGBTI+ human rights defenders, whose work and ability to return to Turkey safely also depends on the end to the targeting of LGBTI+ human rights defenders. As one of the strongest supporters of Türkiye’s accession, Germany should actively support the freedom of association and LGBTI+ human rights in Türkiye.




Our demands




Therefore, the undersigned organisations operating in Germany urge the German foreign ministries to:







Call for the immediate release of all LGBTI+ people and activists imprisoned under the recent operations, 




Demand an end to the raids, arrests, and the repression of LGBTI+ civil society in Türkiye,




Use all available diplomatic channels including through your counterparts in Ankara, calling on them to cease the operations and release all those arrested




Raise the concerns over the torture and inhuman and degrading treatment of those arrested with the Turkish authorities, and call for an end to such treatment,




Provide support for the LGBTI+ civil society in Türkiye through the German Embassy in Ankara, including but not limited to funding and creating safe spaces for engagement.







LGBTI+ rights are human rights and defending and working to protect these rights is not a crime. Ensuring the protection of these rights is the responsibility of all states, including Germany, as a member of the Council of Europe and a signatory to the European Court of Human Rights.




Your support makes change possible




We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.




Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: TGEU
title: Joint Statement: Why Portugal’s Self-Determination Act Must Stay
content:
TGEU, IGLYO, OII Europe and ILGA-Europe have submitted joint comments to the Portuguese Parliament on two Bills that would repeal Law 38/2018, the Self-Determination Act, and reinstate the medicalised regime of Law 7/2011: Bill 391/XVII/1, tabled by Chega, and Bill 486/XVII/1, tabled by the PSD. Both parties sit in the ruling government, so together they command the majority needed to pass these Bills into law. We ask Parliament to withdraw both Bills or vote against them in their entirety.




There is no problem to solve.

 The Self-Determination Act works. Between 2018 and 2022, 1,595 people changed their gender marker, more than triple the previous period, and the competent authority, the CIG, reported in 2022 and again in 2026 that it knows of no refusals, no fraud and no misuse. Twelve European countries have self-determination models, some for over a decade; none has repealed them. Where rare problems arose, courts solved them. Legal initiatives that strip people of acquired rights need a demonstrated need, and none exists.




What these Bills would do







Bring back pathologisation and clinical gatekeeping.

 Trans adults would once again have to prove their identity to two multidisciplinary medical teams, undergo years of psychological monitoring and, as drafted, in practice show proof of surgery before the State recognises who they are. The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that no one should have to accept surgery or sterilising treatment to be recognised, and the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe has called for procedures based on self-determination. Worse still, Portugal already struggles with a shortage of professionals in trans-specific healthcare: a procedure requiring two teams, years of monitoring and a surgical pathway would make legal gender recognition effectively inaccessible in practice, squandering scarce medical resources on certifying instead of treating or meeting actual health needs. These Bills would put doctors, not trans people, in charge of trans people’s identities.













Exclude 16 and 17 year olds from legal gender recognition

, despite the existing safeguards (legal representatives, a personal hearing and a capacity report) and no recorded refusals, fraud or abuse. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child requires capacity-based assessment, not fixed age limits. The reality for those affected: every exam, train ride, job application or school registration becomes a forced outing, in a country where nearly three in four LGBTQI students report bullying or insults at school.













Weaken protection of intersex children.

 Portugal made history in 2018 as the second European country to ban non-consensual medical interventions on intersex children. Bill 391 repeals that ban without an adequate replacement; Bill 486’s weakly defined “health exception” could still permit medically unnecessary “normalising” surgeries. Both Bills regress on Recommendation CM/Rec(2025)7, which Portugal helped adopt only very recently in October 2025.













Roll back healthcare and education rights.

 Bill 391 would ban all gender-affirming care for under-18s by statute, overriding the judgment of doctors, parents and the young people themselves, and restrict teaching on gender diversity in schools, an approach the EU Court of Justice has already rejected in its judgment against Hungary. Bill 486 removes the protected ground of gender expression, restricts sports participation by “biological sex”, risks excluding trans and intersex children from youth and school sport, and deletes the right to a social name, which migrants, minors and non-binary people rely on to live as themselves in schools, workplaces and public services.













Rely on outdated, pathologising and stigmatising terminology

 (“gender identity disorder”, “transsexuality”, “hermaphrodites”) that contradicts ICD-11, which Portugal supported, and the human-rights based language that all 46 Council of Europe member States have adopted with CM/Rec(2025)7. Words matter: law that frames people as disorders invites treating them as such.







Not in line with international human rights law




Restricting fundamental rights requires a pressing social need under Article 8(2) ECHR and the Portuguese Constitution. These Bills offer conceptual or hypothetical worries, thinly sourced on Portuguese practice, not demonstrated problems. Rolling back rights people already hold requires full justification and consideration of all alternatives; these Bills provide neither. They would therefore amount to a prohibited regression, in direct conflict with the ECHR, EU law, the CRC and the Council of Europe’s Recommendation on equal rights for intersex persons. They also leave thousands of people in limbo: both Bills say nothing about pending applications or registry changes already made, including those of 16 and 17 year olds.




Our asks




We call on the Assembly to withdraw or reject both Bills in their entirety. Should any reform proceed, Parliament must first hear trans and intersex people and the organisations working with them, with their safety, anonymity and wellbeing fully guaranteed, and carry out a child rights impact assessment.

author: TGEU
title: Trans Murder Monitoring 2026 shows that every 32 hours, a trans person was murdered
content:
TGEU’s Trans Murder Monitoring (TMM) has recorded 273 trans and gender diverse people murdered worldwide over the past year, on average, one murder reported every 32 hours. Murders were reported across 35 countries, the second-highest number since the monitoring began, and for the first time in Romania and Cameroon. In total, TMM has now recorded over 5,500 murders globally since data collection began in 2009. 




TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia publishes the annual update of its global Trans Murder Monitoring project in the lead-up to Trans Awareness Week, ending with the Trans Day of Remembrance (TDoR) on 20 November. 




The TMM project counts only reported murders, and monitoring work is getting harder. The total number of reported murders is under 300 for only the second time in a decade, but the violence has not eased. Shrinking civic space, media and state-backed hostility towards trans people, and cuts to funding make it less likely that a murder is reported and recorded.

author: TGEU
title: A Monitorização de Assassinato Trans de 2026 mostra que a cada 32 horas, uma pessoa trans foi morta.
content:
A Monitorização de Assassinato Trans [Trans Murder Monitoring] (TMM) da TGEU registou 273 pessoas trans e de género diverso assassinadas mundialmente ao longo do ano passado, em média, um homicídio registado a cada 32 horas. Assassinatos foram registados em 35 países, o segundo número mais elevado desde que a monitorização começou, e pela primeira vez na Roménia e no Camarões. No total, a TMM registou até à data mais de 5,500 assassinatos globalmente desde que a recolha de dados começou em 2009.




A TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia publica a actualização anual do seu projecto global Monitorização de Assassinato Trans no âmbito da Semana de Consciencialização Trans, que termina com o Dia da Memória Trans (TDoR) a 20 de Novembro.




O projecto da TMM conta apenas com números registados, e o trabalho de monitorização está a tornar-se mais difícil. O número total de assassinatos registados é inferior a 300 apenas pela segunda vez numa década, mas a violência não terminou. O espaço cívico em declínio, a hostilidade contra pessoas trans incentivada pela media e pelo estado, e cortes a financiamento tornam menos provável que um assassinato seja relatado e registado.

author: TGEU
title: El Trans Murder Monitoring 2026 muestra que cada 32 horas, una persona trans fue asesinada
content:
El Monitoreo de Asesinatos de Personas Trans de TGEU (TMM por sus siglas en inglés) ha registrado 273 personas trans y de diversidad de género asesinadas en todo el mundo durante el último año, en promedio, un asesinato informado cada 32 horas. Se reportaron asesinatos en 35 países, el segundo número más alto desde que comenzó el monitoreo, y por primera vez en Rumania y Camerún. En total, el TMM ha registrado ahora más de 5,500 asesinatos en todo el mundo desde que comenzó la recopilación de datos en 2009.




TGEU – Trans Europa y Asia Central publica la actualización anual de su proyecto global de Monitoreo de Asesinatos de Personas Trans en la antesala de la Semana de Conciencia Trans, que culmina con el Día de la Remembranza Trans (TDoR por sus siglas en inglés) el 20 de noviembre.




El proyecto TMM solo cuenta los asesinatos reportados, y el trabajo de monitoreo se está volviendo más difícil. El número total de asesinatos reportados está por debajo de 300 por segunda vez en una década, pero la violencia no ha disminuido. El espacio cívico se está reduciendo, hay hostilidad hacia las personas trans desde los medios y el Estado, y los recortes de financiamiento hacen menos probable que un asesinato sea reportado y registrado.

author: TGEU
title: TGEU publishes Legal developments on trans-specific healthcare: A review of national case law in the EU
content:
Court cases have been central to advancing the rights of trans people in Europe, but trans-specific healthcare remains largely untested in the courts.




Since the European Court of Human Rights’ earliest decisions on legal gender recognition, strategic litigation has driven many major advances. More recently, rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union on freedom of movement and non-discrimination have further strengthened these gains. TGEU’s 

2026 Trans Rights Map

 also found that national court decisions are increasingly driving progress in trans rights, particularly where legislative and policy advances are stalled or reversed.




Trans-specific healthcare is an exception and is comparatively less litigated at the European level. Trans people across the EU face significant barriers in accessing trans-specific healthcare. Enforcing their rights to healthcare is further complicated by administrative refusals, unclear national regulations, and national court rulings that remain largely unknown. At the same time, interest is growing in using legal tools to advocate for improved access to trans-specific healthcare, and in how courts across the region handle such cases.

author: TGEU
title: Joint statement: We call on Türkiye to end the targeting of trans people and sex workers
content:
Trans women and trans sex workers are being arrested, prosecuted and held in degrading conditions in Türkiye. Since 12 September, the ‘My Family Is Safe’ operation has escalated into a sweeping crackdown on LGBTI communities and civil society, through raids, arrests and prolonged detention. As governments and international institutions turn their attention to Türkiye in the lead-up to COP31, we call on them to act: to press for the release of everyone arbitrarily detained, ensure accountability, and support the communities affected.




ESWA (European Sex Workers’ Rights Alliance)

, 

NSWP (Global Network of Sex Work Projects)

, 

SWAN (Sex Workers’ Rights Advocacy Network)

 and TGEU – Trans Europe and Central Asia strongly condemn the escalating crackdown on LGBTI human rights defenders and communities in Türkiye, including the raids, arrests and ongoing detention of activists and community members. 




We are particularly alarmed by the targeted prosecution of trans women and trans sex workers, and reports of serious mistreatment and degrading conditions in custody. Together with the attention to the attacks against civil society organisations and their representatives, there is an urgent need for attention to the targeting of trans women and sex workers, whose experiences risk being overlooked in the international response. 




We stand in solidarity with our community

author: TGEU
title: Trans activists and stakeholders gather at TGEU’s Pre-Council to advance trans rights in Eastern Europe and Central Asia
content:
On 9-10 September in Ljubljana, Slovenia, 27 trans activists from Eastern Europe and Central Asia (EECA) and international stakeholders came together to ask one question: how do we protect trans people in a region where democracy and human rights are deteriorating?




The second TGEU Pre-Council Strategic Meeting on Trans Rights in EECA took place ahead of TGEU’s 10th European and Central Asian Trans Council. Over two days, participants analysed the rapidly changing political and legal environment, exchanged lessons learned, and explored ways to strengthen cooperation, joint advocacy and coordinated action.

 




The Strategic Meeting brought together three groups with different but complementary types of expertise and mandates: 







EECA trans activists with direct experience working with communities and conducting national advocacy




International stakeholders working on human rights and the rule of law




Allied movement leaders engaged in human rights protection.







Together, they aimed to build a shared understanding of key challenges and possible responses, identify political and legal leverage points for 2026–2027, and strengthen trust and cooperation.

Participants shared strategies for responding to anti-trans policies.

author: TGEU
title: Join the HIV Awareness Week in Berlin to establish the Emergency Support Network
content:
We are organising two free-of-charge parallel training programmes for queer and trans people that will come together on Friday, 20 November, to establish the Emergency Support Network.




This network should help people navigate services, identify realistic pathways to HIV prevention and care, and receive support without having to navigate complex systems alone. We also want to recognise that Ballroom houses, queer and trans collectives, and migrant communities already provide essential care infrastructure. We intend to strengthen these existing relationships, rather than create a parallel system disconnected from the communities themselves.




The initiative is particularly focused on two target audience groups:







Queer and trans people living with HIV who face barriers to accessing healthcare, especially those without health insurance, appropriate documentation, or access to HIV treatment and other essential services.




Queer and trans people on the move, including migrants, refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented people, who face difficulties accessing healthcare, HIV prevention, testing, PrEP, PEP and treatment.







Community HIV Training — 16, 18 and 20 November




This programme is intended for queer and trans adults, particularly queer and trans youth aged 18 and over, migrants, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented people and other people on the move.
